verdicts.why: A technical trading position; it names a market stance without any attitude toward the trader.
A plain culinary description of crumbly pastry; it takes no side on the pastry.
A brief written note; the word records the document's form and nothing about its worth.
A measure of distance by travel time; purely quantitative.
A unit of angular measure; no attitude is possible.
Being sympathetic toward someone is the sense's meaning, not an attitude carried beyond it; the word does not judge the person understood.
Making sense of a language is a plain statement of ability.
A ship's officer is a rank; the word names the position without praising or belittling the holder.
Dealing with a task is neutral; nothing is said about the task or the doer beyond that.
Serving someone is described in a formal but even-handed word; it neither honours nor demeans the servant.
The esteem is the feeling being named, not an attitude the word adds on top; a positive referent is not a loaded word.
The state of being well regarded is named plainly; the word itself does not rate the person.
Filial deference named as a kind of behaviour; the word reports it without approving or mocking it.
Improving someone's condition is the meaning; the word carries no attitude toward the helped or the helper.
Contributing to a result is stated neutrally, whatever the result.
Changing for the better is the sense's content, not a judgement laid over it.
Serving food is a plain hospitable act; no attitude rides on the word.
Taking something for oneself, as in helping oneself, is stated without approval or reproach in the word itself.
Whether something has consequence is a flat statement of importance; the word does not judge the thing.
Physical substance; no attitude is possible.
Printed content named generically; the word says nothing about its quality.
Sitting as judge at a trial is a procedural act; the word takes no side.
Trying on clothes is a plain everyday action.
Judicial examination of a case is described neutrally; no attitude toward the accused or the court.
Causing strain or trouble is the sense's meaning; an unpleasant referent is not an attitude carried by the word.
